title: Esther's scroll and Nineveh's fast
hookLine: Megillah on reading Esther; Taanit on fasts and rain
carry: read from the page; fast toward a change

cards: Say someone knows the whole book of Esther by heart. Every word, every name, every one of Haman's sons. On Purim night they stand up before the congregation, close their eyes, and recite it flawlessly.
A beautiful performance. According to the Mishnah, it doesn't count.
The tractate beside it has its own surprise: a public fast where an elder stands up in the town square and tells the crowd that the fasting isn't the point.

teach.b: Reading and fasting. First, Megillah, the tractate of the scroll. On Purim, Jews hear the book of Esther read from a scroll, and the Mishnah sets the terms.
Read it out of order, and you haven't fulfilled the duty. Read it from memory, and you haven't either. It has to be read from the written scroll, in order.
But for people who speak another language, reading it in that language counts. Strict about the text, generous about the listener. Second, Taanit, the tractate of fasts.
Much of it is about rain: when to begin praying for it in the autumn, and what a community does when the rains don't come. The answer is a series of public fasts.
On those days, says the Mishnah, the ark is carried out into the town square, ashes are put on it, and the eldest among them stands up to speak.
He reminds the crowd of the people of Nineveh, who fasted in the book of Jonah. The verse doesn't say God saw their sackcloth and their fasting.
It says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way." Works. Not the fast.
The fast is the doorway, and the turning is the room.
Third, the two belong together, and Esther shows why.

teach.h: READ FROM THE PAGE; FAST TOWARD A CHANGE.
teach.b: Before she goes to the king, she asks the Jews of Shushan to fast for her. The fast comes first, then the brave act. Reading and fasting: both are real only when something actually changes.

how: On Purim, Jews gather to hear the book of Esther read aloud from a handwritten scroll, often making noise at Haman's name; on public fast days, congregations add special prayers and the Torah reading for fasts.

o: reciting Esther from memory as the purest way
a scroll read in order, and fasts that lead to deeds
a fast kept by reading scripture all day long

games.q: reading and fasting — tap the pairs.
p: the tractate of fasts and rain

s: the Mishnah says reciting Esther perfectly from memory counts
it has to be read from the written scroll, in order.
the Mishnah lets people hear Esther in a language they speak
for those who speak another language, reading it in that language counts.
at the public fasts for rain, the elder praises the fasting itself
he says the verse about Nineveh speaks of their works, that they turned, not their sackcloth and fasting.

games.q: you know the book of Esther by heart. it's Purim night, and the scroll is across the room. what do you do?
o: recite it from memory; every word is right.
read it from the scroll, in order.
games.why: the Mishnah says reading from memory or out of order doesn't fulfill the duty. the words have to come from the page, in their order.

practice: Choose something short, a few verses of Esther, a psalm, a paragraph that matters to you, and read it aloud from the page, in order, slowly enough to hear every word.
Then set it down, sit with your breath, and let one phrase you'd skipped before stay with you.

wordCard.voice: Reading and fasting. Megillah, the scroll read from the page in order, and Taanit, the fasts that point beyond themselves to changed works. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a scroll; on Purim, the scroll of Esther.

carryVoice: Your line: read from the page; fast toward a change. God saw Nineveh's works, not only its fast. See you tomorrow.
